title: From Raster to Portal: Creating and Publishing an EBVCube
text:
Four dimensions, one file





An EBVCube is the standard format for publishing Essential Biodiversity Variables, the standardised measurements the biodiversity community tracks in common. It is a netCDF file organised in a defined way and following the CF and ACDD metadata conventions, so every dataset, whatever produced it, is structured the same way. That is what makes two of them comparable. Unit 1 covers the framework.
The figure shows the tutorial’s own example, dataset id = 1: three entities, each a box whose front face is the world grid, with time running back along the depth axis.


lon
The x axis of the grid. You fix it once, with extent and resolution.


lat
The y axis. Every layer in the file has to share this exact grid and CRS.


time
A single date, or a whole series. The dates you declare must match the layers you add.


entity
The biological unit: a species, a community, an ecosystem.










Metric and scenario are not dimensions, they organise the cubes inside the file. The file as a whole is the EBVCube; inside it, each metric holds one four-dimensional array named ebv_cube, carrying the lon, lat, time and entity dimensions above. A scenario, when a dataset has one, adds a level on top: scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube.
Dataset id = 1 has two metrics and no scenarios, so it holds exactly two arrays: metric_1/ebv_cube and metric_2/ebv_cube.

section: One real dataset, start to finish
text:
One real dataset, start to finish
The tutorial is built around one published dataset, id = 1, that you can open on the live portal. The metadata fields and code chunks work against that file, so what you read here is what you’d get running it yourself.






Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)



id = 1 Community composition 3 entities 2 metrics 1900–2015
Relative and absolute change in the number of bird species at decadal steps, for forest, non-forest and all bird species. Roughly 4 MB, downloaded once and cached locally.
Martins, I., Pereira, H., Navarro, L. (2022). Dataset page · DOI 10.25829/8grx36

library(ebvcube)

ebv_download(id = 1, outputdir = "data/ebv", overwrite = FALSE)

Every later code chunk starts from that file path. To run the workflow against your own data, point it at your own .nc and the rest of the tutorial runs unchanged.

title: From Raster to Portal: Creating and Publishing an EBVCube
text:
Before you start


You do not need prior netCDF experience, Unit 1 covers the concepts. It helps to be comfortable with:

basic R: installing packages and running scripts;
basic geospatial data in R, at the level of terra or raster;
your own biodiversity rasters, or following along with the example dataset.

The portal units also need a free GEO BON account.


Key resources

EBV Data Portal — discover, download and publish EBV datasets.
ebvcube on GitHub — also on CRAN and the b-cubed r-universe.
Package documentation — the full function reference this tutorial builds on.
Format specification — the structural rules behind the format.
GEO BON — what are EBVs? — the canonical definition and the six classes.
Quoss et al. (2022) — the methods paper describing the package.









Working alongside this tutorial. Every code chunk runs as-is against the example dataset. If you are preparing your own dataset, follow the same steps and swap in your rasters and metadata where Units 3 and 4 point it out.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What is an Essential Biodiversity Variable?
An Essential Biodiversity Variable (EBV) is a standardised, derived measurement that captures a key dimension of biodiversity and lets us monitor its status and change over time. The concept was proposed by Pereira et al. (2013) and is maintained by the Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network (GEO BON) (Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network, n.d.). EBVs harmonise many primary sources, field observations, remote sensing, and model outputs, into a common, analysis-ready format. They sit as an intermediate layer between raw observations and the indicators used for assessment, reporting, and decision making.
Think of an EBV as the biodiversity counterpart to an Essential Climate Variable: a small, agreed-upon set of variables that different groups can produce, compare, and combine because they follow the same definitions. That shared standardisation is what makes data from different projects, taxa, and regions consistent enough to track over time.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The six EBV classes
EBVs are organised into six classes, each capturing a different dimension of biodiversity:


Genetic composition
Genetic diversity and differentiation within and among populations.


Species populations
Where species occur and how abundant they are.


Species traits
Physical, physiological and behavioural characteristics of organisms.


Community composition our example
The diversity and mix of species within a community.


Ecosystem structure
The physical build and extent of ecosystems.


Ecosystem function
The processes and productivity that keep ecosystems running.


The dataset we use throughout this tutorial, Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM), belongs to the Community composition class.






Canonical classes vs. what you see on the portal





The six classes above are the canonical classification defined by GEO BON. On the EBV Data Portal you may not see all six at once; the portal lists only the classes for which datasets are currently available. You may also meet finer labels such as Species distribution or Ecosystem disturbance, which are sub-categories within the canonical classes.
Ecosystem services is not one of the six EBV classes. It belongs to a separate, complementary GEO BON framework, the Essential Ecosystem Service Variables (EESVs), which covers the benefits people obtain from nature rather than biodiversity itself. For the official classification, see the GEO BON definitions page.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Why netCDF? The EBVCube format
A single EBV has a value at every location (longitude, latitude), at several points in time, and for each biological entity measured. Stored as separate map images, that becomes an unwieldy pile of files with no built-in context. The Network Common Data Form (netCDF), long used in the climate sciences, instead holds it all in one self-describing file: the data travels together with the information that explains it, units, dates, entities, and projection.
The EBVCube is the standardised, netCDF-based data format defined for EBVs. It follows two established conventions, CF v1.8 (cfconventions?) (how coordinates, units, and time are encoded) and ACDD v1.3 (acdd?) (the attributes portals use to index datasets), plus a few EBV-specific rules set out in the EBVCube format specification.
Every data cube inside an EBVCube shares the same four dimensions, so each pixel carries four pieces of information, where, when, and which entity:


lon
Longitude, or the projected x-coordinate.


lat
Latitude, or the projected y-coordinate.


time
One date or a whole series: annual, decadal, scenario years, irregular.


entity
The biological unit: a species, a group of species, or an ecosystem type.


The entity dimension is what lets a single EBVCube hold data for many species or other biological units at once. Above these four dimensions, metric and scenario groups organise different biodiversity measures or future projections within the same file. We return to that structure in Unit 4.






Figure 1.1: Overview of the EBVCube data model. An EBV dataset combines a hierarchical structure of scenarios and metrics with four-dimensional data cubes (longitude, latitude, time, and entity), and carries standardised metadata following the CF 1.8, ACDD 1.3, and EBV conventions. Source: Quoß et al. (in preparation).
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Touring the EBV Data Portal
All published EBV datasets live on the EBV Data Portal. Throughout this tutorial we use one of them as the running example:






Worked example: Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)
id = 1 Community composition DOI 10.25829/8grx36
Martins, I., Pereira, H., Navarro, L. (2022). Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM) (Version 1) [Dataset]. German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig. DOI 10.25829/8grx36



Open the dataset page and you will find everything that makes an EBV dataset FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable):

a stable dataset ID (1) and a persistent DOI you can cite;
a structured JSON metadata record (title, abstract, EBV class, creators, license, entities);
the netCDF file itself, available for direct download (≈ 4 MB);
an interactive EBV Visualizer for exploring maps and temporal trends without downloading anything.

The three views you will use most are the Discover page (Figure 1.2), an individual dataset page (Figure 1.3), and the live EBV Visualizer. Click either screenshot to enlarge it.

Discover pageDataset pageEBV Visualizer








Figure 1.2: The Discover page showing the EBV class filters and a list of datasets.











Figure 1.3: The dataset page for id = 1, showing its general metadata and the netCDF download button.
















Portal interface as of July 2026. The portal is updated from time to time, so small layout differences are normal; the metadata, DOI, and download are always on the dataset page.



Browsing and inspecting datasets like this is how you find data on the portal. Next, we look at how you work with it.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Where ebvcube fits
The portal is where EBV data is published and discovered; the ebvcube R package (ebvcube2025?; quoss2022?) is how you work with it. It sits on both sides of the portal:


READ
Reading published data
Give ebvcube a dataset’s numeric ID and it downloads the file, lists the cubes inside, and reads, subsets, or maps them, pulling id = 1 into R in a couple of lines instead of a manual download and netCDF wrangling.


CREATE
Producing new data
Starting from your own rasters or model output, ebvcube assembles them into a valid EBVCube, ready to upload and publish on the portal with its own DOI.


Read on one side, create on the other: that round trip is the workflow in the Overview diagram, and the path the rest of this tutorial follows, one step at a time.






Checkpoint. You just inspected dataset id = 1 on the portal, its EBV class (Community composition), its DOI, and its file format (netCDF). If those three make sense, you are ready to install the tools in Unit 2.







Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network. (n.d.). GEO BON. https://geobon.org/. Retrieved July 31, 2026, from https://geobon.org/


Pereira, H. M., Ferrier, S., Walters, M., Geller, G. N., Jongman, R. H., Scholes, R. J., Bruford, M. W., Brummitt, N., Butchart, S. H., Cardoso, A., et al. (2013). Essential biodiversity variables. Science, 339(6117), 277–278.

Before installing ebvcube, make sure you have:
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
R ≥ 4.2.0 required
The minimum version ebvcube supports. Check yours with R.version.string, and if it is older, update R first, or CRAN will refuse to install the package.


RStudio recommended
A free, widely used editor for R. Not strictly required, but every code example in this tutorial assumes you are working in it. Download it here








What about HDF5 and GDAL?





The lower-level libraries ebvcube relies on, HDF5 (for reading netCDF-4 files) and GDAL (for spatial data), install automatically on Windows and macOS: HDF5 comes with the Bioconductor package rhdf5, and GDAL comes with the CRAN build of terra. There is nothing extra to set up.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.2 Installing ebvcube from CRAN
For most users, the released version on CRAN is all you need:

install.packages("ebvcube")

CRAN resolves all of the CRAN dependencies automatically. Three dependencies, however, live on Bioconductor rather than CRAN, so on a fresh machine you will usually need the one-time step in the next section as well.






Other ways to install





Most people should use CRAN. If you need a newer feature, you can install the development version with devtools::install_github("EBVcube/ebvcube", ref = "dev"), or get the binary builds from the b-cubed r-universe. These are covered in the package’s installation guide.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.3 Adding the Bioconductor dependencies
Three of ebvcube’s dependencies come from Bioconductor rather than CRAN, because reading EBVCube files means reading HDF5 under the hood:


rhdf5
Low-level HDF5 read/write, since netCDF-4 is HDF5 underneath.


DelayedArray
Lazy, on-disk arrays so large cubes do not exhaust your RAM.


HDF5Array
Connects DelayedArray to HDF5 files.


If installing ebvcube reports that one of these is missing, install them with BiocManager:

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("rhdf5", "DelayedArray", "HDF5Array"))

You only need to do this once per R installation.






Which Bioconductor version?





BiocManager automatically picks the Bioconductor release that matches your version of R, which is what you want. You can pin a specific release with BiocManager::install(version = "3.22"), but only do so if you have a reason to, each Bioconductor release requires a matching R version (3.22 needs R 4.5.x), so leaving it out is also a safe choice.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.4 Verifying your installation
First, load the package and confirm the version:

library(ebvcube)
packageVersion("ebvcube")

Then open the small example dataset that ships with the package, a subset of the Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM) dataset. Because it is bundled, this needs no download and works offline:

file <- system.file("extdata", "martins_comcom_subset.nc", package = "ebvcube")

prop <- ebv_properties(file, verbose = FALSE)
prop@general$title
#> [1] "Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)"

If the title prints, your installation is working. When you are ready to pull the full dataset from the portal (≈ 4 MB), the same two lines work with a download instead of the bundled file. We do exactly that in the next unit:

file <- ebv_download(id = 1, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
prop <- ebv_properties(file, verbose = FALSE)
prop@general$title







Checkpoint. library(ebvcube) loads with no error, and ebv_properties() prints the dataset title. If both work, your setup is complete and you are ready to prepare biodiversity data in Unit 3.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.1 What ebv_create() needs
ebv_create() does not read your rasters and guess what belongs in the file. It reads a metadata file you prepare first, builds an empty netCDF with exactly the structure that metadata describes, then leaves it for you to fill. Almost all the work happens before you call the function. Three things have to be ready:
The metadata defines the structure of the EBVCube, the data layers provide the values stored within it, and the entity list links each biological unit to its layers.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
A metadata JSON
The file’s identity and structure as text: title, EBV class, license, spatial and temporal coverage, and one entry per metric.
From the EBV Data Portal form (recommended), or built in R with ebv_metadata().


Your data
One 2-D layer (lon × lat) for every entity, time step, and metric, usually a stack of GeoTIFFs or in-memory rasters.
The output of your modelling or analysis.


An entity list
The names of the biological units the file describes, in the exact order the layers are stacked.
You decide it. For id = 1 it is three entities: All birds, Forest birds, and Non-forest birds.









Metadata first, structure second



Whether you generate the metadata JSON from the EBV Data Portal or with ebv_metadata(), review it before running ebv_create(). If you are using the portal, you can return to the form at any time, update the metadata, and download a new JSON file. Once the metadata accurately represents your dataset, use this final JSON file to build the EBVCube.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.2 Dimensions, metrics, and scenarios
An EBVCube organises biodiversity data along four core dimensions. As the data producer, you define each of them when you create the cube:


lon
Longitude, or the projected x-coordinate. Part of the shared grid set through extent, resolution, and epsg.


lat
Latitude, or the projected y-coordinate. Every layer shares this exact grid and CRS.


time
One observation date or a whole series. The range and interval live in the metadata and must match the layers you add.


entity
The biological unit each layer describes, a species, a group, an ecosystem type. Its order must match your layer order.








Metric and scenario are not dimensions, they set how the cubes are grouped inside the netCDF file. A metric is the variable being measured or calculated (e.g. relative change in species richness); every dataset has at least one. A scenario is optional, grouping the same metric under different projected pathways (e.g. SSP1 or SSP5).
Without scenarios the cube sits at metric_1/ebv_cube; with them, at scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.3 Pre-flight checklist
Before building the EBVCube, verify that your data and metadata describe the same structure. You can run these checks while preparing the metadata, through the portal form or with ebv_metadata(). Because the metadata defines the EBVCube structure, resolving inconsistencies now avoids problems later when you insert data with ebv_add_data().


One shared grid
Same extent, resolution, and CRS across every GeoTIFF. Check with terra::rast() and compare.


A deliberate layer count
entities × time steps × metrics (× scenarios). If the product does not match your stack, something is missing or duplicated.


Final, ordered entities
One name per entity, in the same order as your layers.


A chosen fill value
Decide what marks “no data” (the format default is -3.4e+38) and confirm your rasters use it for gaps.


Exact coverage
Start year, end year, temporal spacing, bounding box, EPSG code, the values you enter into the metadata.


Consistent file format
Every layer reads cleanly in terra, with the expected data type and missing-value representation.








Confirm the grid in one step



This is a template you run against your own exported layers, not the id = 1 example we download elsewhere in the tutorial, so point it at your own folder of GeoTIFFs:

library(terra)

# Point this at your own exported layers.
layers <- rast(list.files("path/to/your/tifs", pattern = "\\.tif$",
                          full.names = TRUE))
layers            # inspect extent, resolution, CRS, and nlyr()

If every layer prints the same extent and resolution, and nlyr() matches your expected count, the grid is consistent.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.4 Getting the metadata JSON
Every EBVCube starts from a metadata JSON, and there are two ways to produce one. Which you pick depends on whether you are publishing through the portal or scripting a pipeline.

3.4.1 Path A — the portal metadata form (recommended)
The simplest way to create a valid metadata JSON is the Uploads → New Upload form in the EBV Data Portal. The form is organised into three tabs. Complete the required fields in the first two tabs, then use the third to generate and download the metadata JSON.
Each tab holds more fields than fit on one screen, so the images below show only the top portion of each. Be sure to scroll through the whole form and complete every field marked with a red asterisk (*).

General informationEBV attributesData upload


Title, creation date, a summary, methods, and any related DOIs, among other general fields.






Figure 3.1: New upload — General information.





The controlled-vocabulary fields: EBV class, EBV name, and entity type, chosen from fixed lists so they can’t be mistyped. Below them you add one or more metrics (each with a name, description, and units) and, if your data has them, one or more scenarios.






Figure 3.2: New upload — EBV attributes.





The portal generates the metadata JSON here. Click Download Metadata to save the .json; that file is the input to ebv_create(). This same tab is where you return later to upload the finished netCDF (option 2, “using the R package ebvcube”).






Figure 3.3: New upload — Data upload, with the Download Metadata link.












You need a GEO BON account



The form sits behind a login. Create a free account at portal.geobon.org before you start.




3.4.2 Path B — from R with ebv_metadata()
You can also build the same JSON entirely in R. This fits an automated or reproducible pipeline, where generating the metadata from a script beats filling a form by hand. ebv_metadata() takes one argument per field the form would ask for, writes the .json to disk, and returns its path. The call below fills those fields with dataset id = 1’s own published values, so the example uses real terms rather than invented placeholders. The controlled-vocabulary fields still have to match the portal’s accepted terms, so ?ebv_metadata stays the authoritative reference for what each one takes.

json <- ebv_metadata(
  outputpath            = file.path(tempdir(), "metadata.json"),
  title                 = "Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)",
  summary               = "Changes in bird diversity at 1-degree resolution caused by land use, estimated by the cSAR model for 1900-2015 using LUH2.0 historical reconstruction of land-use.",
  source                = "cSAR model with LUH2.0 land-use projections and PREDICTS-based coefficients.",
  date_created          = "2018-01-01",
  creator_name          = "Ines Martins",
  creator_institution   = "German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv)",
  license               = "CC BY",
  ebv_class             = "Community composition",
  ebv_name              = "Taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity",
  ebv_spatial_scope     = "Global",
  ebv_domain            = "Terrestrial",
  coverage_content_type = "modelResult",
  ebv_entity_type       = "Communities",
  ebv_entity_scope      = "Bird communities",
  time_coverage_start   = "1900-01-01",
  time_coverage_end     = "2015-01-01",
  metric = list(
    list(standard_name = "Relative change in the number of species (%)",
         long_name     = "Relative change in the number of species using 1900 as reference",
         units         = "Percentage points"),
    list(standard_name = "Absolute change in the number of species",
         long_name     = "Absolute change in the number of species using 1900 as reference",
         units         = "Number of species")
  ),
  overwrite = TRUE,
  verbose   = FALSE
)

A few fields to watch:

ebv_class must match one of the classes the portal lists (the canonical six plus Ecosystem services and Cross-cutting), spelled exactly as shown.
coverage_content_type records how the data were produced: modelResult for modelled data, image for direct observation, and a handful of other CF values.
metric is a list of lists, one entry per metric. The example passes two, so the file gains both metric_1/ebv_cube and metric_2/ebv_cube. To add scenarios, pass a scenario argument the same way; leave it out, as here, and the file stays flat.

Both paths end in the same place: a .json on disk that describes the file you are about to build. Whichever you use, open it in a text editor and read it once before moving on. Editing a line by hand is fine, and often quicker than regenerating the whole file for a one-word fix.






Match the JSON to your data, not the other way around



The metadata declares a shape: so many metrics, so many time steps, this grid. ebv_create() builds exactly that shape, and ebv_add_data() refuses anything that does not fit. If the two disagree, correct whichever one is wrong now, while it is still a line in a JSON file.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
section: 3.5 Downloading dataset 1 for a working reference
text:
3.5 Downloading dataset 1 for a working reference
The example dataset from Unit 1 is worth keeping open here: it is a complete EBVCube, so you can compare your own metadata and file structure against a working example, the Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM) dataset (id = 1). ebv_download() returns the path to the file it writes, so we point it at tempdir() and the code runs from any working directory, with no project folder to set up first:

library(ebvcube)

file <- ebv_download(id = 1, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)

ebv_datacubepaths(file, verbose = FALSE)

For id = 1 the paths come back as metric_1/ebv_cube and metric_2/ebv_cube, two metrics and no scenario segment, which confirms what Section 3.2 covered. Read its metadata the same way you did as a consumer, and treat each field as a slot you will need to fill for your own dataset:

prop <- ebv_properties(file, verbose = FALSE)
prop@general$title
prop@general$ebv_class
prop@general$entity_names        #> "All birds" "Forest birds" "Non-forest birds"
prop@spatial$srs
prop@temporal$resolution

Whatever this file declares, yours will declare too. The difference is that here the values are already filled in, and for your dataset you are the one supplying them.






Checkpoint. Your data share one grid, and the number of layers matches entities × time steps × metrics (× scenarios, if any). Your entity list is final and ordered, and you have a metadata JSON on disk, from the portal form or ebv_metadata(), that you have read through. If that all holds, and your metric and scenario structure matches your dataset, you are ready to build the netCDF in Chapter 4.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.1 The inputs
ebv_create() needs two things, and we generate both from the published dataset so the unit stays self-contained:
Every path below is built from tempdir(), so nothing depends on your working directory or on files cloned from the repository. We start by fetching the published cube and reading the structure we need to match:
library(ebvcube)

# Download the published dataset once. ebv_download() returns the path to the
# .nc it wrote, so this works from any working directory.
orig   <- ebv_download(id = 1, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
new_nc <- file.path(tempdir(), "bird_diversity_rebuilt.nc")

# Read the real structure from the published file so the rebuild lines up.
props    <- ebv_properties(orig, verbose = FALSE)
entities <- props@general$entity_names          # the three bird entities, in order
n_t      <- length(props@temporal$dates)         # number of time steps
dcs      <- ebv_datacubepaths(orig, verbose = FALSE)$datacubepaths

entities
dcs
The metadata JSON is the same file the portal gives you when you click Download Metadata on the upload form. For your own data you would download that file, or write it from R with ebv_metadata() — the same call introduced as Path B in Chapter 3. We regenerate it here so this unit runs on its own, then feed the result to ebv_create():
The raster layers are one multi-band GeoTIFF per metric and entity. In your own project these would be the output of your analysis; here we read each cube out of the published netCDF and write it to a GeoTIFF in tempdir(), so the rebuild has something real to fill from. This is the round trip in action — the same layers that went into the published file come back out, ready to go back in:
library(terra)

tif_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "tifs")
dir.create(tif_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

entity_tag <- function(x) gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x))

for (dc in dcs) {
  m <- as.integer(sub("metric_(\\d+).*", "\\1", dc))   # metric number from the path
  for (e in seq_along(entities)) {
    # Read the cube for this entity across all time steps (bands come back as
    # the time steps), then write it out as a multi-band GeoTIFF.
    r   <- ebv_read(orig, dc, entity = e, timestep = 1:n_t,
                    type = "r", verbose = FALSE)
    tif <- file.path(tif_dir,
                     sprintf("metric_%d_%s.tif", m, entity_tag(entities[e])))
    terra::writeRaster(r, tif, overwrite = TRUE)
  }
}
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
A metadata JSON
The structure and attributes of the cube. Downloaded from the portal, or written from R with ebv_metadata().


The raster layers
One multi-band GeoTIFF per metric and entity, holding the actual values.











Generate the metadata JSON (same call as Path B in the previous unit)





metric is a list of lists, one entry per metric, which is how the file ends up with both metric_1 and metric_2.

json <- ebv_metadata(
  outputpath            = file.path(tempdir(), "metadata.json"),
  title                 = "Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)",
  summary               = "Changes in bird diversity at 1-degree resolution caused by land use, estimated by the cSAR model for 1900-2015 using LUH2.0 historical reconstruction of land-use.",
  source                = "cSAR model with LUH2.0 land-use projections and PREDICTS-based coefficients.",
  date_created          = "2018-01-01",
  creator_name          = "Ines Martins",
  creator_institution   = "German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv)",
  license               = "CC BY",
  ebv_class             = "Community composition",
  ebv_name              = "Taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity",
  ebv_spatial_scope     = "Global",
  ebv_domain            = "Terrestrial",
  coverage_content_type = "modelResult",
  ebv_entity_type       = "Communities",
  ebv_entity_scope      = "Bird communities",
  time_coverage_start   = "1900-01-01",
  time_coverage_end     = "2015-01-01",
  metric = list(
    list(standard_name = "Relative change in the number of species (%)",
         long_name     = "Relative change in the number of species using 1900 as reference",
         units         = "Percentage points"),
    list(standard_name = "Absolute change in the number of species",
         long_name     = "Absolute change in the number of species using 1900 as reference",
         units         = "Number of species")
  ),
  overwrite = TRUE,
  verbose   = FALSE
)












Doing the extraction as a standalone script





The book ships this same extraction as scripts/prepare-inputs.R, which writes the GeoTIFFs to data/tifs/ instead of a temporary directory. You do not need it to run this unit — everything above is self-contained — but it is handy if you want the layers on disk as a provenance record, or as a starting point for extracting layers from your own published cube.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
section: 4.2 Writing the empty netCDF with ebv_create()
text:
4.2 Writing the empty netCDF with ebv_create()
ebv_create() reads the metadata JSON and writes a netCDF that has the right shape but no data yet. You supply the entity names and the grid the cubes sit on: the projection (epsg), the geographic extent, and the resolution in degrees. We pass the entity names we just read from the published file, so the rebuild matches it; the grid is global at 1°.

ebv_create(
  jsonpath   = json,
  outputpath = new_nc,
  entities   = entities,
  epsg       = 4326,
  extent     = c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
  resolution = c(1, 1),
  fillvalue  = -3.4e+38,
  overwrite  = TRUE,
  verbose    = FALSE
)

At this point the file is fully structured but every cell still holds the fill value. Check the skeleton before you add anything to it:

ebv_properties(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)@general$entity_names

ebv_datacubepaths(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)

The entity names should match what you passed in, and the datacube paths tell you where the data will live. For dataset id = 1 there is no scenario layer but two metrics, so the paths come back as metric_1/ebv_cube and metric_2/ebv_cube.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.3 Adding your data with ebv_add_data()
Each cube is filled from its own GeoTIFF, one metric and entity at a time. We wrote those layers to tif_dir in the extraction step above, named by metric and entity, so here we loop over the datacube paths and add each one. The time steps live in the GeoTIFF’s bands, so timestep and band both run 1:n_t.

for (dc in dcs) {
  m <- as.integer(sub("metric_(\\d+).*", "\\1", dc))   # metric number from the path
  for (e in seq_along(entities)) {
    tif <- file.path(tif_dir,
                     sprintf("metric_%d_%s.tif", m, entity_tag(entities[e])))
    ebv_add_data(
      filepath_nc = new_nc,
      metric      = m,
      entity      = e,
      timestep    = 1:n_t,
      data        = tif,
      band        = 1:n_t,
      verbose     = FALSE
    )
  }
}

You can call ebv_add_data() again on the same cube to fill in more time steps later. It appends rather than overwrites, as long as each call keeps the (metric, entity, timestep) combination unique.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.4 Correcting an attribute with ebv_attribute()
If you later spot a wrong unit, a typo in a description, or any other attribute that needs fixing, you can edit it in place without rebuilding the file:

ebv_attribute(new_nc,
              attribute_name = "units",
              value          = "Percentage points",
              levelpath      = "metric_1/ebv_cube")

ebv_properties(new_nc, "metric_1/ebv_cube",
               verbose = FALSE)@ebv_cube$units
#> [1] "Percentage points"

The levelpath argument points at the layer you want to change. Pass "metric_1/ebv_cube" for the cube itself, "metric_1" for the metric, or "/" for a global attribute.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.5 Species-level datasets with ebv_create_taxonomy()
Use ebv_create_taxonomy() when each entity in your dataset is an individual species. Unlike ebv_create(), which takes a simple vector of entity names, ebv_create_taxonomy() expects a CSV file describing the taxonomy of every species.
Each row represents one species, and each column represents a taxonomic rank, ordered from the highest to the lowest level. For example:



order
family
genus
scientificName




Passeriformes
Corvidae
Corvus
Corvus corone


Passeriformes
Paridae
Parus
Parus major



The last column must contain the entity names used in the EBVCube. During creation, this taxonomy is stored in the netCDF alongside the data and can later be retrieved with ebv_properties() under @general$taxonomy.
For maximum interoperability, use Darwin Core names for the taxonomic ranks (for example, order, family, genus, and scientificName). You can also include a taxonomy identifier, such as a GBIF usageKey, to link each species to an established taxonomic backbone.






Row order matters



Your taxonomy CSV must contain one row for each entity in the same order that the entities appear in your data. This ensures that each species is linked to the correct layers in the EBVCube.



# Columns run from the highest rank to the lowest, and the last column holds
# the entity names. In practice this table usually comes from a GBIF or
# Catalogue of Life export.
taxonomy <- data.frame(
  order          = c("Passeriformes",   "Apodiformes", "Falconiformes"),
  family         = c("Hirundinidae",    "Apodidae",    "Falconidae"),
  genus          = c("Hirundo",         "Apus",        "Falco"),
  scientificName = c("Hirundo rustica", "Apus apus",   "Falco peregrinus")
)
taxonomy_csv <- file.path(tempdir(), "taxonomy.csv")
write.csv(taxonomy, taxonomy_csv, row.names = FALSE)

new_nc_tax <- file.path(tempdir(), "bird_diversity_taxonomy.nc")

ebv_create_taxonomy(
  jsonpath   = json,
  outputpath = new_nc_tax,
  taxonomy   = taxonomy_csv,
  sep        = ",",
  epsg       = 4326,
  extent     = c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
  resolution = c(1, 1),
  fillvalue  = -3.4e+38,
  overwrite  = TRUE,
  verbose    = FALSE
)

From here ebv_add_data() works exactly as it did above. The taxonomy is read-only metadata and does not change how you fill the cubes. See ?ebv_create_taxonomy for the accepted column names and separator options.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
section: 4.6 Confirming the rebuild matches the original
text:
4.6 Confirming the rebuild matches the original
Because we rebuilt a file we already have, we can check the two against each other instead of just trusting that the code ran. ebv_analyse() reports the mean and the number of valid pixels for a cube; run it on the original and on the rebuild, and the numbers should agree:

orig_stats <- ebv_analyse(orig,   "metric_1/ebv_cube", entity = 1, verbose = FALSE)
new_stats  <- ebv_analyse(new_nc, "metric_1/ebv_cube", entity = 1, verbose = FALSE)

orig_stats[c("mean", "n")]
new_stats[c("mean", "n")]

If the mean and the valid-pixel count match, your ebv_create() → ebv_add_data() pipeline reproduced the published cube exactly. That is the check that turns “it ran without error” into “it produced the right file.” You can run ebv_properties() and ebv_datacubepaths() once more for a full readout of the finished structure:

ebv_properties(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)

ebv_datacubepaths(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)







A visual check with Panoply





Panoply is a free NASA viewer for netCDF and HDF5 files. Drag your new .nc into it and it shows the group hierarchy, dimensions, and attributes side by side, and it can draw a quick map of any cube. It is a fast way to see whether the file looks right before you hand it to the portal, without writing any more R.









Checkpoint. You wrote an empty EBVCube with ebv_create(), filled its cubes with ebv_add_data(), and confirmed with ebv_analyse() that your rebuild reproduces the published dataset. With a valid .nc in hand, you are ready to validate and visualise it before sharing, in Chapter 5.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading
text:
5.1 Check the structure
Start with the two functions you already met. ebv_datacubepaths() lists every cube in the file, and ebv_properties() reports the metadata slot by slot. Read them against what you meant to build:
ebv_datacubepaths(nc, verbose = FALSE)

props <- ebv_properties(nc, verbose = FALSE)
props@general$entity_names     # the entities you declared
props@spatial$extent           # c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
props@temporal$dates           # the time axis
The datacube paths should list every metric and entity you expect, the entity names should read correctly, and the extent and dates should match your data. A missing entity or an empty time axis points to a step that went wrong in creation.
crumbs: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading

title: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading
text:
5.2 Check the values
Structure can be right while the numbers are wrong, so read a slice and look at its range. ebv_analyse() returns summary statistics for a cube or a subset:

stats <- ebv_analyse(nc, dc, entity = 1, timestep = 1, verbose = FALSE)
stats[c("min", "max", "mean", "n", "NAs")]

n is the number of valid pixels. If it is zero, or NAs covers the whole grid, the cube never received its data. A min or max far outside what your variable should hold usually signals a unit problem or a stray fill value that leaked into the data.
crumbs: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading

title: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading
text:
5.3 See it — map and trend
Numbers only tell you so much; a picture catches problems a summary hides, like data in the wrong hemisphere or an all-empty ocean. This is where ebvcube shines — two one-line functions turn a cube into a figure with no plotting or projection code of your own.

Map a slicePlot the trend


ebv_map() draws a single time step as a classed choropleth, optionally overlaying country borders. One look confirms the data sit where they should:

ebv_map(nc, dc, entity = 1, timestep = 1, classes = 9, verbose = FALSE)



ebv_trend() collapses the spatial dimensions to one value per time step and draws the trajectory. It does double duty — it plots and returns the underlying numbers, so a flat line, a break, or an implausible jump is easy to spot and the values are yours to keep:

trend_vals <- ebv_trend(nc, dc, entity = 1, method = "mean", verbose = FALSE)
trend_vals










If the map looks shifted by 180°



The file is using the [0, 360] longitude convention while the basemap expects [-180, 180]. Read the slice and wrap it before plotting:
r <- ebv_read(nc, dc, entity = 1, timestep = 1, type = "r")
r <- terra::rotate(r)
crumbs: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading

title: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading
text:
5.4 Compare against your metadata
Finally, confirm the file says what you told it to say. Read the attributes back and check them against the metadata form (or the ebv_metadata() call) you used to create it:

props@general$title
ebv_properties(nc, dc, verbose = FALSE)@ebv_cube$units

The title, units, entity count, and time coverage should all match your metadata. If a unit or description is wrong, fix it in place with ebv_attribute() from Chapter 4 rather than rebuilding the file.
crumbs: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading

title: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading
text:
5.5 A pre-flight checklist
Before you move to the portal, walk through this list. If every box ticks, the file is ready to upload:

The datacube paths list every metric and entity you expect.
Entity names, dates, extent, and resolution match your metadata.
Units and the cube description read correctly.
A map of at least one slice looks right, with no 180° shift.
Value ranges are plausible and the valid-pixel count (n) is not zero.

The portal runs its own validation when you submit, but clearing these first saves a round trip. Panoply, introduced in Chapter 4, is a quick way to eyeball the structure outside R if you want a second opinion.






Checkpoint. Your file’s structure, values, map, and trend all match the dataset you meant to create, and every box in the pre-flight checklist is ticked. If so, you are ready to upload it to the EBV Data Portal in Chapter 6.
crumbs: 5  Validating your EBVCube before uploading

title: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.1 Back to the upload form
The submission uses the same New Upload form you met in Chapter 3. Sign in with your GEO BON account and reopen your draft under Uploads. The General information and EBV attributes tabs are already filled from earlier, so the only tab left to finish is Data upload.
crumbs: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.2 Uploading your netCDF
The Data upload tab offers two ways to submit: a ZIP of GeoTIFFs, or a netCDF built with the ebvcube package. You built the netCDF, so choose that option and upload your .nc file.






Add a preview image



If the form asks for one, a small map of a single slice exported from ebv_map() is enough — it makes your dataset easier to recognise in the catalogue. The portal runs its own validation on upload; if it flags anything, work back through the checks in Chapter 5, fix the file, and upload again.
crumbs: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.3 Submitting for review
Once the file is in, submit the dataset for review. It moves out of Draft into a review state, where the portal team checks the metadata and the file against the EBV standard before it goes public. Expect a wait, and possibly a request for small changes. When it is approved, the dataset is published: it appears in the public catalogue and becomes downloadable with ebv_download().
crumbs: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal
section: 6.4 After publication: DOI, citation, and versions
text:
6.4 After publication: DOI, citation, and versions
On publication the portal assigns your dataset a DOI and generates its citation, both shown on the dataset page. You can see this on the live page for the running example, dataset id = 1, where its version history, DOI, and citation all appear.






Cite the dataset, not the package



Point people to the dataset DOI when they cite your data — not to the ebvcube package citation, which credits the software rather than the dataset. If you later revise the data, upload it as a new version instead of editing the published one. The portal keeps versions distinct, so anyone who already cited the earlier DOI still lands on the exact data they used.


Here is that page, embedded live (in the HTML version of the book):



If the page does not load, open dataset id = 1 on the EBV Data Portal.







Checkpoint. Your netCDF is uploaded, submitted, and, once approved, live on the EBV Data Portal with its own DOI. If anything snagged along the way, Chapter 7 collects the fixes for the problems that come up most often.
crumbs: 6  Uploading the dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.1 Installation
These are the problems that stop library(ebvcube) from loading. The full setup is in Chapter 2.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
The Bioconductor packages are not found





there is no package called 'rhdf5' (or DelayedArray, or HDF5Array). These live on Bioconductor, not CRAN, so install.packages("ebvcube") cannot pull them in on its own:

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("rhdf5", "DelayedArray", "HDF5Array"))

Then retry library(ebvcube).









package ‘ebvcube’ is not available for this version of R





You are on an older R, and Bioconductor releases are tied to specific R versions. Either update R to the current release, which is the cleaner fix, or install an older ebvcube that supports your R version:

devtools::install_github("EBVcube/ebvcube@v0.5.0")   # adjust the tag










HDF5 library version mismatched





Your installed rhdf5 was built against a different HDF5 library than the one loaded at runtime. Reinstall it from a clean R session:

remove.packages("rhdf5")
BiocManager::install("rhdf5", force = TRUE)
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.2 Preparing data and metadata
Most metadata trouble comes from the controlled vocabularies. See Chapter 3 for the full form.






A metadata value is rejected





Fields such as ebv_class, ebv_name, and ebv_entity_type accept only the terms the portal knows. If ebv_metadata() or the upload form refuses a value, it almost always does not match one of those terms. Copy the wording from the portal form’s pick lists, or check ?ebv_metadata for the accepted list, rather than typing your own phrasing.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.3 Creating the cube
Errors here usually mean the metadata and the data disagree about shape. The build itself is in Chapter 4.






entities length does not match metadata





The entities vector you passed to ebv_create() has a different length than the entity count declared in the JSON. Fix one so the two agree.









ebv_add_data() fails with a dimension mismatch





The GeoTIFF you are adding does not sit on the same grid as the netCDF, so its resolution, extent, or CRS is off. Reproject it onto the netCDF’s grid before adding it:

target_r <- ebv_read(new_nc, "metric_1/ebv_cube",
                     entity = 1, timestep = 1, type = "r")

r  <- terra::rast("your_data.tif")
r2 <- terra::project(r, target_r)          # match CRS, resolution, extent
terra::writeRaster(r2, "your_data_aligned.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

Add your_data_aligned.tif instead of the original.









Units, titles, or descriptions look wrong after ebv_create()





You do not need to rebuild the file. Fix the attribute in place with ebv_attribute(), as shown in Chapter 4.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.4 Reading the file back
These come up when you validate your file or read a published one. The checks are in Chapter 5.






ebv_read() says “Not enough RAM”





The cube you asked for is larger than the package thinks your machine can hold. Two ways out: subset it spatially first with ebv_read_bb() or ebv_read_shp(), or read it lazily with type = "da" to get a DelayedArray. Note that ignore_RAM = TRUE only switches off the safety check; it does not make the read lazy.









ebv_read_shp() returns an array full of NA





Two usual causes. Either the shapefile is in a different projection from the netCDF, so reproject it to match:

shp_p <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_read(shp), 4326)
sf::st_write(shp_p, "shp_wgs84.shp")

Or the shapefile and the file’s extent do not overlap at all. Compare them before reading:

ebv_properties(nc, verbose = FALSE)@spatial$extent   # c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
sf::st_bbox(sf::st_read(shp))










The map looks shifted by 1800b0





The file uses the [0, 360] longitude convention while your basemap expects [-180, 180]. Read the slice and wrap it with terra::rotate(), as described in Chapter 5.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.5 Uploading to the portal
The submission steps are in Chapter 6; here are the snags that interrupt them.






The upload is rejected





The portal validates your file when you upload it. If it pushes the file back, the fault is almost always something the pre-flight checks in Chapter 5 would have caught, so re-run those, fix the file, and upload again. A very large file can also be slow or time out; before you assume the portal is at fault, make sure the file is not larger than it needs to be.









A value you need is not in a pick list





The form’s controlled vocabularies are deliberate. Choose the closest listed term rather than forcing your own, and if nothing fits, ask the portal team through the contact route on the dataset page rather than working around it.









The dataset is stuck in review





Review is done by people, so it takes time, and a request for small changes is normal. If a long stretch passes with no word, follow up through the dataset page contact or GEO BON.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.6 Getting help and reporting bugs
If none of the above fixes it, a good bug report is the fastest way forward. Package bugs go to the GitHub issue tracker, and a report the maintainers can act on includes:

the output of sessionInfo(),
a minimal reproducible example, ideally on a dataset that ships with the package,
the full error message, and
what you expected to happen.

For open questions rather than bugs, use the GitHub Discussions board. Before posting either, check you are on the latest release with packageVersion("ebvcube"), since the fix may already be out.






Citing and licensing



To cite the package, run citation("ebvcube"), which prints both a plain-text and a BibTeX entry; to cite a dataset, use its own DOI from the portal page rather than the package citation (see Chapter 6). The package is open source under GPL-3, with the source on GitHub, so pull requests are welcome.








Checkpoint. You can find the stage where you got stuck, apply the fix, and, if it turns out to be a genuine bug, file a report the maintainers can act on. That closes the whole arc, from a raster on your disk to a published dataset with a DOI. For further reading and references, see Chapter 8.
